sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
Why I imagine that my grandmother told my mother in the late 1880's because she died, my grandma died at the turn of the century and they lived in the Hartleton section, in the country part of Hartleton section and these stories, are merely, most of them heresay. You can't prove it about the people who lived there and if I did know, I wouldn't tell. But there were many little stories about the whichcraft and for instance now, there was a man and his wife living together and but she was always rather a mysterious woman and the neighbors didn't seem to like her very well and that was the day when people were suspicious of witchcraft. A great deal was going on like that and she would visit in people's homes and the babies would start to shriek and cry in their cradles especially if she was jealous of that family or if she had some trouble with them or was jealous in any way, see? Then she would put the hex on that baby and sometimes the baby got very ill suddenly or it would just start to, cry and cry. And time went on and there came a time when they blamed her for being a witch but they didn't tell her so until a number of years went by and these same things would occur and so one day when she was at one of these houses visiting and the baby was so bad, so ill I should say, and the mother said, "Why do you hex my baby?" She just put it to her and at first she pretended she didn't know what she was talking about. Then their conversation drifted so that she left the lady whom she was visiting to believe that she was a witch, although she didn't just say so, but she talked to her and she said, "Please take the hey" or whatever you call it, "Off of my baby". And she didn't say whether she would or she wouldn't but she said, "I must go home", and she left quickly and as soon as she left, the baby stopped crying, the instant of that. And the same thing would appear like that it was very ill, if it had a bad fever, they would coax her, tell her to take the hex off, and when she did that, the baby got well. So they were sure that she was a witch. And the husband knew about this but he hadn't any proof because she never, as I say, troubled him but he wanted to know whether she was or not and so finally he got talking around about witchcraft and maybe it would be nice to be a witch and do all these things and get even with people you didn't like and all this and that, and the day finally came when she said to him. "Would you like to be a witch?" He said, "I sure would". Well, she said, the time went by again and she didn't admit it and finally the day came when she said, If you want to be a witch, she said, "I can tell you what to do to be one" She said, "If you do exactly what I do, and say what I say." Well, he thought for a while and he said, "Well," he said, "If you're a witch, don't see why I can't be a witch, we live in the same house. We can both be witches". So she said, "Well, now, we’ll have to go out to the dungyard." That's what they called it. They didn't call it a barnyard, it was a dung- and there was quite a pile of dung, and so she gave him a pitchfork and she took a pitchfork. "Now", she said, "We'll go around this dungpile 3 times and the last time you say what I tell you to say. She said, "I'm going to tell you to say 'I give myself into the hands of the devil'. Alright. So they got the pitchforks in the position she wanted them and they started and went around once and twice and when they come around to this spot where they were to stop and say it, they started to say it together. And she said. "I give myself into the hands" and he said, "God Almighty" And she said of course. "Into the hands of the devil" and she dropped dead, 1
Side 1 153R and he lived happily everafter, but they got rid of the witch. Now that was supposed to be true, but he wanted to know if she really was a witch and she was. Now these people up there didn't see it. This is a story of heresay. I think most of them are. That's one. And I was trying to think of these. Now this is just about an incident up there. I don't think it's witchcraft but the people thought it was terrible what happened. There was a man who was drunk nearly all the time and his wife was very unhappy and she had a dear little dog that she liked, so well, and he was always . . . when he'd get drunk, then he would abuse his wife and she was also pregnant.at this particular time of this incident and he was very, very drunk one night and he got after the dog and she said, "Oh, don't take it out on the dog", she said. She says "That's one of my the things that I enjoy most, that little dog", she said, and he knew that she loved that little dog so he took it out on the dog and he got mad and he shot the dog between the eyes. and killed it and when her baby was born, the little boy was blind and he never gained his eyesight. And the neighbors all blamed it on what he had done. Now, we don't know whether he could have gotten help at that time, probably could have gone to the city and they could have, you know, taken X-rays and dome something about it. We don't know but the child is buried in the Hartleton Cemetery. You don't need to say that if you don't want because they'd know who it was.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: How old did the child live to be then?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Not very old! Died quite young. Then there was another incident where some people believed that what women see or are frightened when they're pregnant, that something will harm their child and mama's grandmother told her that she heard this was a true fact that a woman who was so terribly frightened at seeing a snake that her baby had a head of a snake and that she nurses this baby and it had a mouth and a head like a snake but it did not live very long. It seemed that she didn't nurse it even very long and everything that she nursed it, she'd cover it with a cloth so she wouldn't be able to see it and some of the people came there of course out of curiosity to see it but it was a ghostly and a terrible experience. And that baby didn't live long. Now we don't know whether there's any truth in that or not but to this day, I know a lot of people who still believe that you can look things off or have experience like that. You don't often hear about it but we don't know if it's true or not. Now that's supposed to have happened, oh, around here somewhere, I don’t know.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: You say your mother's grandmother told her that?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Yes, oh, that would have been back in that would bave been the,my grandma, my grandma died before 1900 and her mother would have been, I don't know how long she lived but it least would have been you might have said 70 years back cause they lived to be about 70 along in there. Can you hear that on here?

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Yeah, I think so, yes.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
Cause you could figure it out yourself then. Then there was one lady who tormented the people. She'd make all sorts of noises and if people were having a party, say, in those days they had so many cornhushing bees and they'd get together and sew carpet rags together. Now that's what they called it, "carpetrags", and they'd make them into balls and they weren't as careful as they are today with them but they had fun and it seemed that this lady, now I'm not sure whether she was one of them,seemed to me that she ws one of them and then she'd excuse herself to leave, whether she went out to what they called the "outhouse" or what I don't know, but she went someplace and then they would be annoyed. And she would, there'd be a noise under the door and there would be a cat stick her paw under there and wiggle and make 2
Side 1 153R this noise and they got tired of this and this happened so often, and one of the men saw her and he said the next time that happened he was gonna cut that paw off so he was ready and the next time that happened they cut this cat's paw off and the next morning, this woman walked around with her hand off. That's right. I didn't see it so I can't prove it but it's what's supposed to have happened and let's see, I think I have another one here. I was thinking about this just a while ago. Well, then, this happened to my mother. She lived on a farm and they told her that it was spocked but she wasn't afraid of that and she lived with an old gentleman whose sister had died recently and he was alone and in those days you could very easily instead of paying rent, you know, live with this man and cook for him, so she and had and the baby, must have been long ago because it was my oldest brother and he would be in the 90's if he were living, and she said she heard all kinds of noises and one was she used to iron out in what they called a "sunkitchen" away from the main house, especially in the summer naturally. And she would be ironing away there and there would be just like switches go all over the floor, all over her feet under the ironing board. It would be just like the wind and she told the man of the house about that and he said, "Oh, don't worry about that, that’s just my sister” he says. “She comes back to trouble me”. And so my dad said, "Well, we'll fix that, we’ll just lock that door with a bolt so that they can't come in, they can’t come into the door, can't, because the door was tight, tight sils,” (here comes somebody) but that didn't keep them out. (think I'll see what they want) So he said, "I'll put a lock on there what they called a leather lock, it was leather, heavy leather across. He nailed it in on this side and that side because up until that time, they just had an ordinary little, these latches that (you probably never saw one) it's shaped like your thumb and it was fastened and you'd let your thumb on there and then you'd go like that and that would, lifted the latch, as very old-fashioned latch.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: I've seen that.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Yes. Well, that didn't do any good because that would go click, click, click and then this noise would start. The door would just open and then this noise would start and mother said, "I'm not gonna be frightened to death", she said, "I'm gonna stay here and iron so the next night she was there again and my father had nailed this heavy strip across and when the time came, for this with everything just separated. The nails just came out of that just as if it was nothing and the latch went click, click, the door opened and came this swishing wind and this noise like switching. Do you know what I mean by switch? It's, well, switch - went all over the floor, made this awful noise and be right under her feet.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: But she couldn't see anything?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
Couldn't see a thing. And she said, "Oh, I'm not gonna stand anymore of this, I'm gonna leave, so she said she grabbed the baby and left the ironing board and said I never went back into that kitchen to do any work in the evening because it always happened in evening. And this gentleman said, "That's just my sister, Josephine, she comes back to trouble me “and he said, “Now, tonight at a certain time,” he said. ”I wasn't going to tell you this but I'll tell you" (they had their own graveyard on the place, a lot of people did) he said, "You look, you'll see her this white image, sailing from the graveyard. Her feet never touch the ground and yet she's not up in the air but she's just like that and she's dressed in white" and he said she didn't have white on when she was buried so he said, ""That I can't understand, but,” he says, “She’ll come over and then all at once you’ll hear these noises. You don't see 3
Side 1 153 R her come in the house, you don't hear her come in, but he said "When she's through with her development, you’ll just see this white image again sailing over the field and go up to this graveyard and disappoint". And that went on they said until that house was torn down and a new house built, and that seemed to end that trouble. That's the story of that one. I have one more and that's all I can think of. This one was a hand-me-down too of long ago. It seemed that this family living in this brick house it was a very old house and nobody wanted to live in this house because it was haunted. They said that a little boy came down every evening when the woman would be getting supper and stand by the fireplace. It was in the days when they did most of the cooking in the fireplace with their kettles and the (that they hung on. What was that that they hung them on?) iron to come out to hang them on, iron, oh, I know

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: I know what you mean.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: The kettles, the thing they hang on, and he'd stand there and nobody ever touched him because they were afraid. They said they understood that you should never touch a spirit, but he'd stand there and he was a sweet looking little boy and he would beckon them with his finger for them to follow him, like this. He would take his finger and go like that. He wanted them to follow him and they said why they couldn't follow him because they understood that he'd disappear and they didn't know what would happen to them. But this one family said they weren't afraid. They went into the house and lived there and this thing happened every night for quite sometime. And this one lady said she made up her mind one time she was going to follow him because she said he looked so sweet and nice she didn't think how he could hurt her and she just wanted to see what would happen and she said I didn't give him my hand, she said i gave him the corner of my apron and she said it got black, immediately, the corner of that apron but it didn't burn. And she said "He didn't go up the chimney he didn't disappear, he walked through the house and I went with him and he went to the attic, and went over to this big chimney that was built from the ground up, see, outside, and he stopped in front of this chimney and pulled out several bricks and more bricks until he came to a box. And he handed this box to this lady and then he disappeared. And he was never seen after that and this box was full of money. Now they think that he was bribed or in some way, he had stolen this money and it worried him, and the spirit came back and presented itself in this manner until someone took him up and he gave it away, gave it back. Now that's the spook stories I have to tell you.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Did anybody say what he looked like? Was he like rosy checked or was he white, could you say?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: He was a very beautiful child, very beautiful boy, very beautiful. His hair was a little long but he was very sweet and fair and she said he had beautiful eyes and always looked so pleading, so pleading because he wanted them to come. That went to show that if it were a spirit, that he wanted to be at rest. That's the way those people presented it in those days and they believed it too. The people that told these stories girlie, believed these things. Now we don't beleive it today, but they did. Now there's a gap that must be filled somewhat or other between then and now that we don't know how to do.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Is this house still standing that that happened in?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
No, I don't even know where it was. Don't even know where that was. 4

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Did you say that people told these stories when they'd be sitting around in the evenings or . . ?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Yes, they'd have these husking bees and rag cutting, things like that and they'd tell these stories and usually try to outdo each other. Each one would try to tell one better or worse. It seemed to be the thing they wanted to do in those times and . .

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: This rag cutting, was that to make braided rugs?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Yes. They would cut them in pieces and on those nights, all they did was take materials there,old blankets and old clothes and if they were making woolen rug, then of course you had to have all wool and if you were making a cotton rug, the cotton rugs were made more carelessly than the other. Now they were just cut into pieces and wrapped together until they had balls, and they didn't make the balls too big because then they were easy to handle. Then when the ladies started to make the rugs, before they made them, they'd sew them together, you see, and some would put them together and make balls of them and they were all sewn together. Others sewed them as they needed them had their needle and thread ready, see.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Some ladies would collect a whole ball full and some would just do it as they went along?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
Yes, that's right. I know I made some rugs when I was first married and I made out of old underwear that my father-in-law wore, wore them in the wintertime, and it was wonderful material for rugs. I asked a lady about next door that made rugs, and she said "That's wonderful" and she dyed them for me a lovely shade of pink and then I had black and it was pink and black. And I could cut pretty long pieces. And this old lady next door said prefer to leave them in short pieces and stitch them as you use them because you might want to trim them, one might be wider than the other and . . to meet whatever you have to meet." And I was telling this Mrs. Styers that makes these rugs, do you know who I mean? She goes around making rugs and she was at one of these houses that I, well visiting homes some weeks ago and I says to her, that I was one of the patronesses of one of those houses, hostesses because my father was born in the house and she thought it would be nice if we were hostesses, we were dressed in colonial costumes and we received the people and explained to them her antiques that she had. Course she was hostess too. Well, anyway this Mrs. Styers that you want to hear about she's a young woman, lives here in town and she makes beautiful rugs and she was out in the backyard with her sewing machine and all her outfit, samples of rugs - you should go and see the rugs. Where was she that I saw her, someplace in Lewisburg the other day, I'm not sure. Well, anyway, and I was telling her about this rug I made and she laughed. I said I had made it til I believe I had about 2' wide and I thought it was so beautiful, pink and black. . I'd make about 6 strands of pink and then maybe 2 of black and then pink and black, you know, and I laid it on the floor and I said the middle came up in a peak. And she said, "You stitched it too tight" so she taught me, I watched her how she put the needle in and when you sew the braids together. And she said, "What did you do with that peak?" Well, I said "I was just a little provoked about it and I didn't know what to do"so I said "I just took the whole thing out", I left the outside be but I took it all out until this peak, until it lay flat, then I took that apart abd did it over, and she said, "Well, that's about the only way you could do". And that was my experience in making rugs. I never made any after that. started one and I started to hook one too and I didn't finish it. It got too 5
Side 1 153R complicated.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Did this rugmaking parties go on in your grandmother's day too?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Oh, yes, they made a lot of them. My mother made them and people today, a lot of our girls here in town make them even.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Do you know if your mother's grandmother made them too?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Oh, yes, indeed they did.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Cause that went way back.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Way, way back. My mother told me one time that an old lady told her that in colonial times, people who couldn't afford carpet that they scrubbed their boards with soft soap, a soft soap is the water that gathering the boiled soap that you make. When they boiled soap, there was water under it and that was pure lye. Now they'd scrub these boards until they were almost white - beautiful, and then she said they would put straw on the floor in the wintertime to keep the boards warm. Now not many people know that and she said it had it good points and it had its bad points because she said you'd slip easily on that. You could imagine, you put straw or hay on top of smooth flooring it would slide with you and she said you had to keep it far away from the fireplace. Many a home burned down from that, but she said it was a way to keep the floors warm. They didn't have carpet.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: They didn't make any rag rugs or anything?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
They didn't - they evidently didn't then. No, and she said the first oil cloth that they could . . . they didn't call it linoleum, they called it oil cloth that old people told her about, this my auntie had told me when we were sitting up here in the cabin in the mountain where we used to tell things, stories and she said they'd take a large piece of cloth that they had woven, themselves, you see, and they would soil it with, I'm not sure I'm telling this right, but it's interesting to know anyway, they'd soaked it with linseed oil and tar and then linseed oil and tar until they had it pretty thick until they could still handle it. Then they would nail it up to the side of the barn and if they could, they would put more layers on; if they couldn't they'd leave it like that until the sun had it . . . they'd have to watch it very closely, that they didn't put it on the hot sunny side of the barn cause that would melt the tar, but where it would keep cool and that's the way they made the first oil cloth to put on their floors. But not many people know about that. Now how successful it was, she said she didn't know because it wasn't long after that until they took the mens' old shirts and trousers and they cut them up and braided them see, and made some rugs for the floor, but they didn't put them on top of the straw because they would slide right away. They had to take the straw off the floor then and do away with it and but the . . . these rugs that they made. How well they were made, I don’t know. And I don't know now when the crocheting came in or the knitting but I know that they used to make oldfashioned needless, homemade needless to hook their rugs. They'd take a piece of steel and stick it in wood. I have one out here that belongs to an old lady (I"ll show it to you after a while) that I tried to use and I . . . . her grandmother is living and I told her sometime I was going to give it to her because she should have it, but the point I wanted to make is everything was homemade. They had to find a way to meet what they needed. That's the point of all this stuff. They had to meet it, they had to find out some way to meet their needs whether it was for the floor or the 6
Side 1 153R bedding or what. And as time went on, why things got beautiful and then of course, they made quilting frames, wasn't long til they had nicer patches and they wanted some nice things on their beds so they started piecing the little scraps together, they did little designs, and I think the first designs were made according to the width of the patch that they had. If they just had little slivers they had to make little designs and if they had larger pieces, then they could have made larger squares. That's the way.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: They used that when that . . . I think they used it twice,once when my brother cut his leg terribly. They were in the country and couldn't get the doctor and another time, a tooth bled so terribly and that did work! Now I think the reason it worked was because they believed that it would. If they didn't believe that it would, I don't think it would have worked. You and I could say that and if we didn't believe it, why it would be nothing. But they believed that it would work.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Did they consider that powwowing, to stop blood like that?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
Uh uh. That was faith in God. That wa s faith in God. That is faith healing, Now powwowing - I wish I could find that book that I got from Harrisburg - I gave it to Jeannette a while and Idon't know if she give it back or not. Oh it had everything in it, the Indians did, (673) how the Indians cured people and how it was done with herbs. Now herbs is a different thing. Course some of their herbs that they used in that time, we don't use today, but there is a plant grows called either - I was talking to a professor in Lewisburg, Mr. (he's a retired professor) well, I can't think of his name. I'm 80 years old so you must pardon me if I don't remember everything. Who was I talking to . . what's his name . . ? Well, anyway, he has it growing in his yard. We would call it just a wood but it comes up and it has a little leafshaped . . like that . . and if you open it up just at the right place you can blow in there and it'll be like a little pillow, see? It's called "live for ever" in one book and another book it's called "life everlasting". I forget the botanical name, it's in that book I got from the state and that is the plant that my mother and neighbor used by the bushels to get on my brother when he was bitten by a rattlesnake. Now that happened about 1908 or '09 here in Mifflinburg. See my sister and I are the youngest of the family of 8 and this boy that was bitten is still living and he's 86 years of age, lives in Minneapolis. And he was a boy at that time around here and he was out with a group of men for huckleberries and he was just a young kid and they cornered this rattler. Rattlers love to be where there's huckleberry bushes and they cornered this rattler and they had a pointed 9
Side 1 153R stick at it's head, like that, to hold it and then they got my little brother I call him little, he was little then, to cut these rattlers cause it had a lot of rattlers on, and while he was cutting these rattlers, he felt this sting and he said, "I'm bitten", and they said "Why you couldn't be, because we have this head in a vise", you know, and to this day when anybody, I don't think anybody's living, that was out there at that day, out with them, but you talk to him, he says "I don't know how it happened because I didn't see another snake" but they said positively another snake must have bitten him, that was nearby. And one man there said, "I have good teeth". Now that you read in the book that you get from the state, they say you shouldn't do it but they did in these times and it didn't hurt the man either. He said, "I have perfect teeth far as I know". He said, "I'll suck it out" and so he sucked and sucked and he thought he had all the venon but I don't think he had because it started to swell up terrible and they had whiskey with them just for that purpose and they did the wrong thing again by giving him a lot of whiskey to drink which carried the poison through his system quickly. He should not have had a speck of whiskey. And until they got him down from the mountain, and I went through this experience, got him to Mifflinburg to the doctor, his arm and hand was thick and the doctor said. "My, oh my, we should have had this boy long ago". Well, to make the long story short he was all summer getting rid of that, the result from that smakebite. And the doctor fed him poison, you ever hear of that, poison to kill poison? They gave him poison internally which my mother kept on a very high shell so none of us kids would get it and they used this poultice - that's a point I want to bring out - because they believed and the doctor believed too that the poultice drew out more of this poison than the medicine. And it had to be pounded. They put it into a wooden tub and pounded it with a wooden . . . . well, like you would a oldfashioned potato master. Did you ever see an oldfashioned potaoto...well, they took that and (813) wood on wood, see, so there would be no acid from tin or anything like that, and this was crushed so fine and they took that and made a poultice and wrapped his arm and hand in that and they did that oh, I think for about 2 weeks. And the neighbors came together and helped my mother and the men went to the mountain in the laurel and around and gathered this need. Side 2

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
I was young enough to know that it was something very unusual. I thought it was wonderful the way the people came to see him and I told the people that I was doorkeeper. The people came to see this boy's arm. Over a hundred people came to see him because everybody thought he was going to die. At that time we had a stove in this room, an oldfashioned stove with a pipe that went through the ceiling. Now you probably have never experienced that and never will. And this was one of the smaller pipes and we - it was only about like that anyway and his arm was as thick as that pipe. The doctor never expected him to live but this poultice did a marvelous job and he got so much better and he was all summer getting well. And I remember the day first they thought they'd have to take off his arm and then his hand, then his finger and I guess the good Lord was with him because they didn't need to take any off and I remember the day when the two doctors took all the old skin off of his arm and hand, see it died, it was dead, it ws dark and ugly and..but he gave credit to the poultice of that weed called either "live for ever" or "life everlasting" same meaning. That's what they used. And I know there was a very heavy doctor bill and the man with whom he was with that got him to do this, said "I will pay the doctor bill". I remember the day, it was my mother wept when she heard that because they never knew how they was ever going to pay because there was two doctors attending him. One was Dr. Staves here in town and Dr. Bickey. They're both dead now. The Staves were brothers, one, Dr. Ralph, was a doctor in Lewisburg and Dr. Charlton in Mifflinburg, and it's peculiar how they called them Dr. Ralph and Dr. Charlton Staves, and Mr. Bickley was the son of the dean of Gettsburg College, the seminary there they went for..preachers, we call pastors. Lutherans call them pastors, and he was dean so they were very 10
Side 2 153R prominent people and they took special - the point I want to make is that these doctors took special interest in this boy because it was a dreadful thing and they said that they had done everything wrong at the mountain. And how we can learn today never give them any liquor no matter how much pain they have or anything. Don't give them any liquor because that drives it right through your system. But he lives, but I saw for my own eyes and everybody else that every year during the dog days (now there's such a thing as dog days) and this happened during the dog days, that for years there was a shadow came up just like this when it was the right side, it ws the right arm that was bitten, it would come over about this far, just a shadow, a dark shadow, every year at dog days, and he says the last time we were out there visiting, he was quite old then, he said, "Every time the dog days comes around, I feel something strange." He says, "I don't know," he says "I think its imagination" but he says, "I feel it" and he outgrew of course, the . . that shadow. But he said, "For years, that shadow came". Now that is a true story. It's no witchcraft, it's no powwowing, it’s nothing. it's something that happened. I think there's a lot of strange things that happen today people don't think anything about. They just go on and say, well that'll go away and it does.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: What about powwowing? What was that?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Well, I don't know, the powwowing that I know of, the little bit of powwowing that I know of I think was more, more faith than powwowing, but they called it powwowing. This woman, well, she powwowed for my sister, the one that was here. She had decline, what they call decline in those baby days and she had pneumonia and the doctor didn't know how this thing was gonna' turn out. He gave her so many days to make a turn for the better and she did get better but she stayed very, very delicate and she wasn't right, I mean she didn't seem to be getting along as she should. She didn't.. well, she wasn't well, that's all but she was still the baby and this lady who lived here in town did powwowing. She called it powwowing and she came to the house, we knew her quite well cause she used to wash for mother and did some ironing too, and she said if you will let me powow for Myrtle, she’ll get better and mama didn't believe in powwowing. Mother said, "well", she said "I'll think about it" and so she talked it over and mama said, "I made up my mind that whatever she would do I would think it was God's will" but she said, "That whatever He's doing, she believes", but she powwowed. She took a piece of string (I think I told this to Jeannette) and measured her. She measured her heighth and her width everyway that she could, she would measure her, and then she took this string and folded it up as much as she could til it would fit into the latch of a door. She took the door off of its hinges, (I bet you heard this before, did you?)

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: I've heard something like it.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: And then she put this string in that huge and she said, "Now as this hinge wears out this string, cuts it, you know, wears it from opening and closing the door or rusts whatever it is, Myrtle will get well and she’ll thrive and be a healthy baby and she was! She got well and she ws a very healthy baby. healthy child.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: She only had to do this one time?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Just once.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Do you know if she gave her any tea or anything?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
No, she didn't give any to her : she'd be too young to drink tea. She was a baby, not even with a spoon, nothing. And she went around and did powwowing. 11
Side 2 153R How many she did or whether it was varied and different, that I don't know.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: You don't know whether she powwowed for different kinds of things or was it just for babies?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: She powwowed for different kinds of things, uh huh, but I don't know any of those stories but there might have been . . . just anything, anything that people had and if they believed in it. Now mother believed in It but she believed in it from a different way.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: How's that? You mean . . .

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: She believed in it if it was to be so, God would do that. And this woman, she believed that too but she called it powwowing. That was exactly powwowing for her. She didn't say anything about God at all.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: So did powwoing have like a bad name or..?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Well, it more or less went with whichcraft in those days long ago, but I think the day came when powwowing was more faith healing. I think it is today.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: So you think at one time it was more connected with witchcraft?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Yes. I do.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: And then it kind of separated away from that.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Yes, that's right.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: If it would have been connected with whichcraft then, it would be like the same person who was a witch would do powwowing too, or . . . ?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: No, they just did devilish work. They were possessed.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: The people who did witchcraft and the people who didn't powwowing?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: No, not powwowing. Powwowing was a little different from this wicked witchcraft. From what I understand and from the stories that I read, powowing was more of a help to people. They helped them and they never talked about it. They didn’t say that they got it from the angels, spirits, they said, "I can do it". "I can do it", I can doit", and they said "I can teach you how to powow and the people who powwow today down at York and around there, those people still say that they can teach you how to powwow.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Did you ever hear anything about a man had to teach a woman and a woman had to teach a man?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: No, except this woman was trying to teach her husband that I told you about.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: The witch?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: The witch. She didn't teach any women up there because they didn't want to be it. They had enough with her.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Are there any people around today that you know of that are still doing things like this, either powwowing or...?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab:
No. I don't, not right here in Mifflinburg. Well there's a lot of people go to these summer camps, these . . . there's one called The Order of St. Luke 12
Side 2 153R that here in America is . . well, all churches go there in the summer. And they are trained to believe in faith healing.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: What was this woman's name who powwowed for your sister?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: I hate to give it to, but it was a Mrs. Baker, but she has relatives living right here in town. You see that happened in my sister's time.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: When would that have been?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Well, now she was born in1902 and just that same winter and in that year: it happened in1902 in Mifflinburg you could say but I won't say Mrs. Baker. Did the other people give their names to you?

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: Yeah. Was that a Mrs. Stewart Baker?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: No. no. There's a Mrs . . . . She had a son named Eddie, I know. She has grand- children living around here and they know it. They know that their grandma did that.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: What did they think of that? Do you know?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: I don't know what they thought at the time, but right now, I think they just laugh at it. But I belong to a Lutheran Church and I know that we don't believe in anything like that - in powwowing or even that extreme faith healing like you say, I go here and my arm is broken and something is wrong and I come out and it’s healed, nothing like that.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: I wanted to ask you. Do you know of any ministers or . . who would have been around in the old days that like would have had experience with this or would have known about this or . . ?

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: They couldn't help but have known about it and I think they were very much against witchcraft and powwowing. I think all they believed in was you was to pray, get on your knees and pray and ask God in the name of Jesus that if it his will, to heal what was wrong or to help it. Nowadays a lot of people say if God is willing, but I was taught years ago that's the wrong way to say it. I have two brothers that are ministers - one's a Presbyterian and one a Methodist and of course, I'm a Lutheran but they became pastors of those churches because they educated them and then they - when they were in college, so then they went to their churches. Well, anyway, I know when my brother came home one time and we were talking about that and he said, "Don't ever say if God is willing". He said "That's putting God cheap." He said “God is always willing to do what is right. Don't say if God is willing, say, if it is God's will", if it is His will, so and so will happen". If you say, "Oh, I'm gonna’ go some place tomorrow if God is willing, he said, “always say if it's God's will". Course now they got that in their education at the seminaries how to express themselves. That's how he taught us when we take communion, to always take your bread and your cup in your left hand because it's nearest to your heart. Little things like that. Hold your Bible in your left hand and turn the pages with the right and things like that.

sp.speaker: Barbara:
sp.ab: That's interesting.

sp.speaker: Olive:
sp.ab: Course I didn't mean to say that on here, but I just put that in. But I think it's . . I thought of that expression right away "If God's willing". Why of course He's willing to do anything that's right. But if you come from the Old Amsbach, the old Reimensnyder, that old Reimensnyder that lived to be so very old, I met him when I was a kid. 13
